name: ECG 2 · The reading method
blurb: Read rate, rhythm, intervals and axis on any ECG, every time.

topics.name: Rate
topics.desc: Count the heart rate from the grid, regular or irregular.

cards.q: The R waves are exactly five large squares apart. The rate is
cards.a:
60 bpm

Five large squares are 1 second; one beat per second is 60 per minute.
cards.note: Thaler ch3 p.124–125; Khan ch2 Table 2-2

cards.q: Put the rates in order for 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 and 6 large squares between R waves
cards.a:
300 → 150 → 100 → 75 → 60 → 50

Each value is 300 divided by the number of large squares.
cards.note: Thaler ch3 p.125–126; Khan ch2 Table 2-2

cards.q: R waves are 2.5 large squares apart. What is the rate?
cards.note: Thaler ch3 p.126, 129; Khan ch2 Table 2-2

cards.q: There are 25 small squares between R waves. What is the rate?
cards.note: Thaler ch3 p.126; Khan ch2 Table 2-2

cards.q: The next R falls between the third and fourth heavy lines. The rate is about
cards.a:
Between 100 and 75

Three squares is 100 and four is 75, so the rate lies between them.
cards.note: Thaler ch3 p.126

cards.q: Explain: Under 60 is slow, over 100 fast
cards.a: The resting heart normally beats 60 to 100 times a minute. Below 60 is bradycardia; above 100 is tachycardia.
cards.note: Thaler ch3 p.119, 128

cards.q: Explain: Three to five squares is normal
cards.a: Khan’s shortcut: if R waves are between three and five large squares apart, the rate is 60–100 and needs no exact sum. Calculate only when it falls outside that window.
cards.note: Khan ch2 Table 2-2

cards.q: Explain: Irregular rhythm: count six seconds
cards.a: When RR intervals vary, no single interval gives the rate. Count the QRS complexes in 6 seconds (two 3-second marks, or 30 large squares) and multiply by 10.
cards.note: Thaler ch3 p.127; Khan ch2 Table 2-2

cards.q: Explain: Slow rates: divide or count
cards.a: For a slow rhythm both methods still work: 300 ÷ large squares (8 squares ≈ 38 bpm, 10 squares = 30 bpm), or a 6-second count × 10. Khan also allows a 5-second count × 12.
cards.note: Thaler ch3 p.126–127; Khan ch2 Table 2-2

topics.name: Is it sinus?
topics.desc: Prove sinus rhythm and judge regularity with four questions.

cards.q:
A regular rhythm from the sinus node at 120 bpm is normal sinus rhythm.
True or false?
cards.a: False. It is sinus, but over 100 bpm it is sinus tachycardia, not normal sinus rhythm.
cards.note: Thaler ch3 p.119, 128

cards.q: Explain: A P before every QRS
cards.a: The first proof of sinus rhythm: one P wave before every QRS, and a QRS after every P. Every atrial beat reaches the ventricles.
cards.note: Thaler ch8 p.334–335; Khan ch2 p.35

cards.q: On a sinus strip, the PR interval from beat to beat is
cards.a:
The same in every beat

A sinus impulse takes the same path through the AV node each time, so the PR is fixed.
cards.note: Thaler ch3 p.124; Khan ch2 p.35

cards.q: Name the lead where a sinus P wave is always inverted
cards.a:
aVR

aVR looks at the heart from the right shoulder, opposite the direction of atrial depolarisation.
cards.note: Thaler ch3 p.132; Khan ch2 Table 2-1, ch3 p.81

cards.q: Which pair of leads shows P waves best for judging rhythm?
cards.a:
II and V1

Khan names II and V1 as the best leads to see P waves.
cards.note: Thaler ch3 p.122; Khan ch2 p.35, ch3 p.82

cards.q: Explain: Regular means equal RR intervals
cards.a: A rhythm is regular when the RR intervals are equal along the strip. In sinus rhythm the PP intervals are also equal, and equal to the RR.
cards.note: Khan ch2 p.35

cards.q: Explain: Irregularly irregular: no pattern at all
cards.a: When RR intervals vary with no pattern whatsoever, the rhythm is irregularly irregular. The classic cause is atrial fibrillation, covered in level 3.
cards.note: Thaler ch3 p.150; Khan ch11 p.281

cards.q:
A rhythm whose RR intervals alternate short, long, short, long has no pattern.
True or false?
cards.a: False. Alternating intervals repeat predictably; that is a pattern, unlike atrial fibrillation.
cards.note: Thaler ch3 p.150; Khan ch11 p.281

cards.q: Put Thaler's four questions in order
cards.a:
Are normal P waves present? → Is the QRS narrow or wide? → How do P waves relate to QRS complexes? → Is the rhythm regular or irregular?

Thaler asks them in this order for every rhythm.
cards.note: Thaler ch8 p.329, 334

cards.q: Explain: Normal sinus rhythm answers all four
cards.a: For normal sinus rhythm the answers are: P waves present, QRS narrow, one P for every QRS, rhythm regular. Any different answer flags an arrhythmia to work out.
cards.note: Thaler ch8 p.334–335

topics.name: Intervals
topics.desc: Measure PR, QRS and QT, and correct the QT for rate.

cards.q: Explain: Normal PR is 0.12–0.20 s
cards.a: Measure the PR from the start of the P to the start of the QRS. Normal is 0.12–0.20 s, three to five small squares. Khan accepts up to 0.22 s in adults.
cards.note: Thaler ch1 p.62; Khan ch2 Table 2-1

cards.q: Explain: A long PR exceeds 0.20 s
cards.a: A PR over 0.20 s (more than one large square) is long. When every P still conducts, this is first-degree AV block, covered in level 4.
cards.note: Thaler ch8 p.338; Khan ch2 p.35

cards.q: A PR of 0.10 s is
cards.a:
Short

Anything under 0.12 s (three small squares) is a short PR.
cards.note: Thaler ch8 p.341; Khan ch2 p.43

cards.q: Which QRS duration is normal?
cards.a:
0.08 s

A normal QRS is 0.06–0.10 s; 0.12 s or more is wide.
cards.note: Thaler ch1 p.70, ch8 p.334; Khan ch2 Table 2-1

cards.q: A QRS of 0.14 s should first make you think of
cards.a:
A bundle branch block

Khan: QRS 0.12 s or more means bundle branch block is present until proven otherwise.
cards.note: Khan ch2 p.35; Thaler ch8 p.339

cards.q: Explain: QT runs from QRS onset to T end
cards.a: The QT interval runs from the start of the QRS to the end of the T: all of ventricular depolarisation and repolarisation. Measure it in a lead where the T end is clear and there is no U wave.
cards.note: Thaler ch1 p.72; Khan ch10 p.228

cards.q: At a rate of 75, the RR is 0.80 s. The QT should be less than
cards.a:
0.40 s

Khan’s rough rule: QT under half the preceding RR interval.
cards.note: Thaler ch1 p.72; Khan ch10 p.228

cards.q: QT is 0.36 s and RR is 0.64 s (√0.64 = 0.8). What is the QTc?
cards.note: Thaler ch7 p.301

cards.q: Explain: Upper limits of the QT
cards.a: Khan’s table, no formula needed: at 66–100 bpm the QT should be under 0.41 s in men, 0.43 s in women (under 0.47/0.48 s at 45–65 bpm). Thaler: on QT-prolonging drugs the QTc must not exceed 500 ms.
cards.note: Khan ch2 Table 2-5; Thaler ch7 p.301

cards.q:
A prolonged QT can predispose to a life-threatening ventricular arrhythmia.
True or false?
cards.a: True. Delayed repolarisation is the substrate for torsades de pointes.
cards.note: Khan ch10 p.228; Thaler ch3 p.121

topics.name: Axis
topics.desc: Find the QRS axis with leads I and aVF, then refine it.

cards.q: The QRS axis is measured using
cards.a:
The six limb leads

Axis is defined in the frontal plane, which only the limb leads record.
cards.note: Thaler ch2 p.85–86

cards.q: Lead aVF is positive when the axis lies between
cards.a:
0° and 180°

aVF sits at +90°, so any axis within 90° of it, 0° to 180°, is positive.
cards.note: Thaler ch2 p.87–88

cards.q: Explain: I and aVF both positive: normal
cards.a: The quadrant method: if the QRS is mainly positive in both I and aVF, the axis lies between 0° and +90° and is normal.
cards.note: Thaler ch2 p.88; Khan ch2 Step 9

cards.q: By Khan’s table, what is the normal axis range for a 55-year-old?
cards.a:
−30° to +90°

Khan gives −30° to +90° for adults over 40.
cards.note: Thaler ch2 p.86, 90; Khan ch2 Table 2-1, ch9 p.213

cards.q: Explain: I positive, aVF negative: left
cards.a: QRS positive in I, negative in aVF puts the axis between 0° and −90°: left axis deviation. Khan reserves the term for −30° to −90°.
cards.note: Thaler ch2 p.92; Khan ch9 p.213

cards.q: I positive, aVF negative, II positive. By the −30° rule the axis is
cards.a:
Normal

A positive lead II keeps the axis within −30°, inside the extended normal range.
cards.note: Thaler ch2 p.90; Khan ch9 Table 9-1

cards.q: Explain: I negative, aVF positive: right
cards.a: QRS negative in I, positive in aVF puts the axis between +90° and 180°: right axis deviation. Khan sets the adult threshold higher, at +100° to +110°.
cards.note: Thaler ch2 p.91; Khan ch2 Step 9, ch9 p.214

cards.q: Explain: Both negative: extreme axis
cards.a: QRS negative in both I and aVF puts the axis between −90° and 180°. Thaler calls this extreme right axis deviation; it is rare.
cards.note: Thaler ch2 p.93

cards.q: aVL (−30°) is the most equiphasic lead, and I and aVF are positive. The axis is
cards.a:
+60°

Perpendicular to aVL is +60° or −120°; a normal quadrant makes it +60°.
cards.note: Thaler ch2 p.90; Khan ch2 Table 2-4

cards.q: Match each cause with the axis it tends to produce
cards.a:
Left anterior fascicular block: Left axis deviation
Right ventricular hypertrophy: Right axis deviation
Pulmonary embolism: Right axis deviation
Left ventricular hypertrophy: Left axis deviation

Khan lists LAFB and LVH under left axis, RVH and PE under right axis.
cards.note: Khan ch9 p.214–215

topics.name: The step-by-step read
topics.desc: Read every ECG in the same order and write the report.

cards.q:
Experienced readers can skip the system and go straight to the obvious abnormality.
True or false?
cards.a: False. Both books insist on a fixed, methodical order so that nothing important is missed.
cards.note: Thaler ch8 p.327–328; Khan ch2 p.35

cards.q: The standard calibration mark should be
cards.a:
10 mm for 1 mV

Both books: 1 mV is displayed as a 10-mm deflection.
cards.note: Thaler ch8 p.328; Khan ch2 p.77

cards.q: Why does Khan assess rhythm before rate?
cards.a:
Rhythm is clinically more important

Khan: rhythm is more important clinically, and a normal rate is easily spotted.
cards.note: Khan ch2 p.32, 35

cards.q: Why does Khan look for bundle branch block and WPW before the ST segment?
cards.a:
They can mimic or mask infarction

LBBB obscures ischaemia and hypertrophy; RBBB and WPW can imitate infarction.
cards.note: Khan ch2 p.32–33, 43

cards.q: Khan checks the ST segment at step 4, ahead of the T waves and axis, because
cards.a:
Acute infarction depends on it

Early diagnosis of acute MI hinges on careful assessment of the ST segment.
cards.note: Khan ch2 p.33, 51

cards.q: Put Khan's steps in order
cards.a:
Rhythm and rate → Intervals and blocks → ST segment → Q waves → T waves → Axis → Arrhythmia

Khan: 1 rhythm/rate, 2 blocks, 4 ST, 5 Q, 8 T, 9 axis, 11 arrhythmia.
cards.note: Khan ch2 p.33–34

cards.q:
In Khan’s method, the axis on its own establishes a specific diagnosis.
True or false?
cards.a: False. Khan calls the axis ancillary: it supports a diagnosis but makes none alone.
cards.note: Khan ch2 p.34

cards.q: Put Thaler's nine steps in order
cards.a:
Rate → Intervals → Axis → Rhythm → Conduction blocks → Pre-excitation → Enlargement and hypertrophy → Coronary artery disease → Other conditions

Thaler measures first (rate, intervals, axis), then works through rhythm and each disease group.
cards.note: Thaler ch8 p.328–329

cards.q: "Sinus rhythm 72/min, PR 0.16 s, QRS 0.08 s, QT 0.38 s, normal ST and T, normal ECG." What is missing?
cards.a:
The axis

Rate, rhythm, intervals and ST/T are there; no axis is stated.
cards.note: Khan ch2 Fig. 2-2F

cards.q: Which is one of Khan’s four closing statements?
cards.a:
Borderline ECG

Khan’s four: normal, within normal limits, borderline, abnormal.
cards.note: Khan ch2 p.35

topics.name: Normal variants
topics.desc: Recognise findings that look abnormal but are normal.

cards.q: Explain: Sinus arrhythmia follows breathing
cards.a: Sinus arrhythmia is sinus rhythm that is slightly irregular: the rate rises on inspiration and falls on expiration. It is a normal finding.
cards.note: Thaler ch3 p.129–130

cards.q: Loss of sinus arrhythmia is classically seen in
cards.a:
Diabetic autonomic neuropathy

Diabetes can damage the autonomic nerves that vary the sinus rate with breathing.
cards.note: Thaler ch3 p.130

cards.q:
A resting rate of 42 bpm in a fit marathon runner can be normal.
True or false?
cards.a: True. Thaler: rates of 35–40 bpm are common and normal in well-trained athletes.
cards.note: Thaler ch3 p.119, ch8 p.348

cards.q: Which feature fits benign early repolarisation?
cards.a:
A notched J point

A notched or slurred J point with concave ST and no reciprocal change is typical.
cards.note: Thaler ch6 p.249–250; Khan ch2 p.52, ch5 p.123

cards.q:
T inversion in V1–V3 in a healthy 19-year-old can be a normal variant.
True or false?
cards.a: True. Inverted T waves in V1–V3 are normal in children and young adults.
cards.note: Thaler ch6 p.246; Khan ch8 p.193, 202

cards.q: Name the lead where an inverted T wave is always normal
cards.a:
aVR

aVR faces the heart from the right shoulder, so its T is normally inverted.
cards.note: Thaler ch6 p.246; Khan ch8 p.193, 202

cards.q:
A narrow Q in lead III alone, with none in II or aVF, means an inferior infarction.
True or false?
cards.a: False. Khan: an isolated narrow Q in III without Q waves in II and aVF is a normal variant.
cards.note: Khan ch1 p.16, ch2 p.61–62, ch6 p.139

cards.q: A healthy 25-year-old has an rSr' in V1, QRS 0.07 s, no slurred S in I or V6. This is
cards.a:
A normal variant

A narrow QRS rSr' without a slurred lateral S is a normal variant in over 5% of people.
cards.note: Khan ch1 p.22, ch4 p.96

cards.q: According to Thaler, the most frequent cause of poor R wave progression is perhaps
cards.a:
Improper chest lead placement

Thaler: perhaps most often, improper placement of the leads on the chest wall.
cards.note: Thaler ch6 p.263; Khan ch2 p.60–61
